title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array: binary search on inflection.
shortTitle: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array: Binary Search on Inflection
keyPoints: A rotated sorted array has two sorted runs with the minimum at the start of the second run (the pivot).
Binary search locates the pivot in O(log n) time by comparing the middle element to the right boundary.
If middle is greater than right, the minimum lies strictly to the right of middle, so set left to mid plus one.
Otherwise the minimum is at middle or to its left, so set right to mid.
Comparing to the right boundary rather than the left cleanly handles every rotation including zero rotation.
For duplicates, when middle equals right, shrink right by one, which degrades worst case to O(n) but stays correct.
Use BigDecimal compareTo for exact comparison of financial rate values.

s1_definition.oneliner: Compare middle to the right boundary and keep the half that still contains the drop point.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Rotated sorted array** – a sorted array shifted so it wraps around at one pivot point, creating two ascending runs.
- **Minimum location** – the minimum sits at the pivot, the single place where a larger element is immediately followed by a smaller one.
- **Binary search on inflection** – compare `a[mid]` to `a[right]`; if `a[mid] > a[right]`, the pivot is to the right, otherwise at mid or to the left.
- **O(log n) time, O(1) space** – each iteration discards half the array.
- **Duplicate handling** – when `a[mid] == a[right]`, shrink right by one to resolve ambiguity.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of interest-rate checkpoints that were sorted ascending but then rotated because the cycle restarted partway through the year. An analyst needs the lowest rate, which sits exactly at the point where the sequence drops from a high back to its restart low. Instead of scanning all checkpoints, the analyst repeatedly looks at the middle checkpoint and compares it to the last one, throwing away half the list each time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array locates the pivot of a sorted array that has been rotated, the single point where a larger element is immediately followed by a smaller one, which is where the minimum sits. You solve it with binary search in O(log n) time and O(1) space by comparing the middle element to the right boundary: if the middle is greater than the right, the pivot must be strictly to the right of middle, otherwise it is at middle or to its left.

Comparing to the right boundary rather than the left is the deliberate choice that makes this clean. Comparing to the left leaves fully sorted or certain rotations ambiguous and forces extra cases, whereas comparing to the right cleanly decides which half holds the pivot in every rotation, including the zero-rotation case where the array is already sorted and the answer is simply the first element.

The senior nuance is duplicates. When values can repeat, the middle can tie with the right boundary and you cannot tell which half holds the minimum, so you safely shrink the right boundary by one, which degrades the worst case to O(n) for an all-equal array but keeps it O(log n) otherwise. For financial rate values, compare with BigDecimal compareTo so exact decimal rates are ordered correctly.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, this is used on interest-rate checkpoints that were recorded ascending but rotated when the rate cycle restarted mid-year, letting the treasury feature find the lowest rate instantly even over a long list.

Remember one sentence: Compare mid to the right boundary, keep the half that contains the drop, and converge to the minimum in O(log n) time.
